title: A Comprehensive Study of Charge-Carrier Mobility in Double Lateral-Gate Silicon Junctionless Transistors
abstract: We give in depth overview of charge-carrier mobility in p-type silicon double lateral-gate junctionless transistors (DLGJLT) through a mix of computer simulations and experimental results. The devices were built on low-doped silicon-on-insulator substrates using atomic force microscope nanolithography. Because the design uses air-gap side gates instead of a gate-oxide layer or junction, it allows electrical current to flow through a lightly doped silicon channel. This setup reduces impurity scattering and protects transport quality from interface damage. We used three-dimensional TCAD Sentaurus simulation tool to model the device's electrical behavior and confirm our experimental data for transconductance and drain conductance. We attempt to give a comprehensive view on the charge transition within the device.
summary: This work comprehensively investigates charge-carrier mobility in advanced silicon junctionless transistors using a combination of experimental measurements and 3D TCAD simulations. The authors analyze how scaling the device geometry—specifically channel width and thickness—affects hole transport, revealing a critical trade-off between achieving high mobility and maximizing carrier drift velocity. The findings provide crucial guidelines for designing next-generation nanoscale electronic devices.
main_problem: The study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of charge-carrier mobility in p-type silicon double lateral-gate junctionless transistors (DLGJLTs). It seeks to establish design guidelines by analyzing how device geometry influences charge transport.
main_result: The paper details a mobility-velocity trade-off: while narrower channels increase drift velocity, they degrade mobility due to enhanced confinement and scattering. Optimal performance requires balancing channel width and thickness.
method: The research combines experimental electrical characterization with advanced three-dimensional TCAD Sentaurus simulations using a hydrodynamic transport model.
model_or_system: The physical system is a p-type silicon DLGJLT built on SOI substrates using AFM nanolithography. The analysis models hole transport, considering effects like carrier heating, non-equilibrium transport, and geometric confinement.
key_observables: Charge-carrier mobility, hole velocity, output/transfer characteristics ($I_D-V_{DS}$, $I_D-V_{GS}$), and drain conductance ($g_D$).
important_parameters: Channel width (30 nm to 100 nm), channel thickness (20 nm to 100 nm), and gate-to-channel air gap (50 nm to 150 nm).
main_assumptions: The hydrodynamic model is used for high-field transport, and discrepancies between simulation and experiment are attributed to non-ideal interface effects like fixed charges.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device schematic, simulated output/transfer characteristics comparing theory and experiment, and plots showing hole mobility dependence on gate bias and confinement.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from presenting the device structure and basic electrical characterization to detailed simulation studies analyzing the impact of geometric scaling (width, thickness) on carrier transport mechanisms and mobility.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state electronics, the detailed modeling of non-equilibrium carrier transport, confinement effects, and scattering mechanisms shares mathematical parallels with open quantum systems or strongly coupled mesoscopic physics.
